formal-solution-5c662fc0.title: Formal Solution

I_\\nu(au_\\nu).name: Radiative Intensity
I_\\nu(au_\\nu).description: The specific intensity of radiation at frequency u and optical depth au_ u . It quantifies the power per unit area, per unit frequency, per unit solid angle.

I_\\nu(0).name: Initial Radiative Intensity
I_\\nu(0).description: The specific intensity of radiation at frequency u at the starting optical depth ( au_ u = 0 ).

au_\\nu.name: Optical Depth
au_\\nu.description: A dimensionless quantity representing the opacity of the medium at frequency u . It is defined as the integral of the extinction coefficient along the path. au_ u = ∫ κ_ u ds , where κ_ u is the extinction coefficient and ds is the path element.

S_\\nu(t).name: Source Function
S_\\nu(t).description: The source function at frequency u and optical depth t . It represents the ratio of emission (including scattering) to absorption coefficients of the medium at that frequency and depth. For thermal equilibrium, S_ u = B_ u(T) , the Planck function.

t.name: Integration Optical Depth
t.description: The dummy variable of integration for optical depth within the integral term. It represents an intermediate optical depth within the medium.

e.name: Euler's Number
e.description: The base of the natural logarithm, approximately 2.71828. Used in the exponential decay function.

$I$.name: Electric Current / Moment of Inertia
$I$.description: The rate of flow of electric charge, or resistance to rotational acceleration.

$\\nu$.name: Kinematic Viscosity
$\\nu$.description: The ratio of dynamic viscosity to density, representing a fluid's resistance to shear flow under gravity.

$\\tau$.name: Infinitesimal Volume Element
$\\tau$.description: An infinitesimal region of space over which a volume integration is performed.

$S$.name: Poynting Vector
$S$.description: The directional energy flux density of an electromagnetic field.

formal-solution-5c662fc0.interpretation: The equation describes the radiative intensity per unit frequency, I_$u(\tau_ u)$, at an optical depth \tau_$u$. The first term, I_$u(0)e^{-\tau_ u}$, represents the initial radiation intensity I_$u(0)$at the starting point ( \tau_$u$ = 0 ) that has propagated through the medium and attenuated due to absorption and scattering, with \tau_$u$being the optical depth. The second term is an integral that accounts for the radiation emitted or scattered into the beam from within the medium. S_$u(t)$is the source function, representing the ratio of emission to absorption (plus scattering) at optical depth t . This term integrates over all optical depths t from the starting point ( 0 ) to the current optical depth ( \tau_$u$), multiplying the source function at each point t by the factor e^{-(\tau_$u - t)}$, which accounts for how much of that internally generated radiation escapes and reaches the optical depth \tau_$u$. The exponential factor e^{-(\tau_$u - t)}$represents the fraction of radiation emitted at optical depth t that survives its journey to optical depth \tau_$u$without further absorption or scattering.
formal-solution-5c662fc0.symmetry_origin: This equation is derived from the differential form of the equation of radiative transfer, which is a fundamental equation in astrophysics and radiative physics. The solution is obtained by integrating this differential equation, often using an integrating factor method. The derivation itself does not typically rely on specific symmetries or conservation laws beyond the conservation of energy and the definition of optical depth.
formal-solution-5c662fc0.limits_and_boundary: If the medium is completely transparent ( \tau_$u\to$ 0 ), the equation simplifies to I_$u(0)$, as expected. If the medium is completely opaque ( \tau_$u\to$ ∞ ) and the source function S_$u(t)$is constant, the first term goes to zero, and the intensity approaches S_$u$, indicating that the radiation is thermalized and reflects the properties of the medium at that point. If there is no source within the medium ( S_$u(t)$ = 0 ), the equation reduces to I_$u(\tau_ u) = I_ u(0)e^{-\tau_ u}$, describing simple attenuation.
formal-solution-5c662fc0.conceptual_definition: This formula represents the formal solution to the equation of radiative transfer, describing how the intensity of radiation changes as it propagates through a medium that can absorb, emit, and scatter radiation. It accounts for both the initial intensity of the radiation and the contributions from emission and scattering within the medium.
formal-solution-5c662fc0.intuitive_summary: The final radiation intensity is the sum of the initial radiation that passed through unhindered and the radiation emitted or scattered from within the medium that reaches the observer.

pinching-force-f4effc14.title: Pinching Force

\\theta_{collimation}.name: Collimation Angle
\\theta_{collimation}.description: The angular half-width of the collimated jet. It represents how tightly focused the outflow is. A smaller angle indicates a more collimated jet.

c_s.name: Sound Speed
c_s.description: The speed at which pressure waves propagate through the plasma or fluid. It is a measure of the thermal pressure support within the jet material.

v_{jet}.name: Jet Velocity
v_{jet}.description: The bulk speed of the plasma forming the jet. This is the characteristic velocity of the outflow.

$\\theta$.name: Angle Coordinate / Polar Angle
$\\theta$.description: The angle displacement, or polar coordinate angle in spherical geometry.

$c$.name: Speed of Light
$c$.description: The maximum speed at which all conventional matter and information in the universe can travel.

$s$.name: Seconds / Proper Time Interval
$s$.description: The SI unit of time, or the invariant interval traversed by a clock.

$v$.name: Speed / Velocity Magnitude
$v$.description: The rate of change of position with respect to time, representing the speed of a particle.

pinching-force-f4effc14.interpretation: The equation$\theta_{collimation} \approx$\frac{c_s}{v_{jet}}$quantifies the angular half-width,$\theta_{collimation}$, of a collimated jet.$\theta_{collimation}$is approximately equal to the ratio of the sound speed,$c_s$, within the jet material to the bulk velocity of the jet,$v_{jet}$. The sound speed,$c_s$, represents the characteristic speed at which pressure disturbances propagate through the fluid. A higher sound speed indicates a more 'pressure-supported' flow, where thermal pressure gradients can resist magnetic confinement, leading to a wider opening angle for the jet. Conversely, a lower sound speed implies that the jet is less susceptible to thermal pressure effects and can be more effectively confined by magnetic forces or other collimating mechanisms, resulting in a narrower angle. The jet velocity,$v_{jet}$, is the bulk speed of the material forming the jet. A higher jet velocity means that the plasma is moving much faster than the speed of internal pressure waves, allowing the jet to maintain its coherence and directionality over large distances, hence a smaller$\theta_{collimation}$. This relationship is often derived in contexts where magnetic fields play a crucial role in launching and collimating outflows, such as in active galactic nuclei or protostellar systems.
pinching-force-f4effc14.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from considering the balance of forces within a magnetized plasma flow. In many astrophysical jets, magnetic fields are responsible for both accelerating the plasma and confining it into a narrow beam. The sound speed$c_s$ represents the thermal pressure scale, while the jet velocity$v_{jet}$ is related to the bulk kinetic energy. The degree of collimation is effectively determined by comparing these two scales: if the bulk motion is much faster than thermal motions ($v_{jet} \gg c_s$), the jet is strongly collimated. If thermal pressure is significant compared to kinetic energy ($c_s \sim v_{jet}$), the jet will be wider. The derivation typically involves MHD (Magnetohydrodynamics) equations, considering pressure gradients, magnetic forces, and the bulk flow velocity. The specific angular width$\theta_{collimation}$ can be related to the ratio of transverse pressure (related to$c_s$) to longitudinal momentum flux (related to$v_{jet}$).
pinching-force-f4effc14.limits_and_boundary: As the jet velocity$v_{jet}$ approaches infinity (while$c_s$ remains finite), the collimation angle$\theta_{collimation}$ approaches zero. This indicates perfect collimation, where the jet is infinitely thin. Conversely, as the sound speed$c_s$ approaches the jet velocity$v_{jet}$ (or$c_s \gg v_{jet}$), the collimation angle$\theta_{collimation}$ approaches 1 radian (or values greater than 1, though the approximation may break down). This implies a very wide opening angle, where the jet is essentially not collimated and behaves more like an isotropic outflow, dominated by thermal pressure rather than directional forces.
pinching-force-f4effc14.conceptual_definition: The pinching force, often relevant in astrophysical contexts like jet formation from accretion disks or plasma physics, describes the tendency of a magnetic field to constrict or 'pinch' a conducting fluid or plasma. The formula$\theta_{collimation} \approx$\frac{c_s}{v_{jet}}$ specifically relates the angular width of a collimated outflow (like a jet) to the properties of the plasma. It suggests that the degree of collimation is determined by the ratio of the sound speed within the plasma to the jet's bulk velocity.
pinching-force-f4effc14.intuitive_summary: A faster jet with a slower sound speed will be more tightly collimated.

homogeneity-0c631165.title: Homogeneity

$\\psi(\\mathbf{x})$.name: Wavefunction
$\\psi(\\mathbf{x})$.description: The quantum mechanical wavefunction of a particle or system at position $\mathbf{x}$. It is a complex-valued function that contains all the probabilistic information about the system.

$\\mathbf{x}$.name: Position Vector
$\\mathbf{x}$.description: The spatial position vector of the particle or system in three-dimensional space. It specifies the location where the wavefunction is evaluated.

$\\mathbf{a}$.name: Translation Vector
$\\mathbf{a}$.description: A vector representing the displacement or shift in space. The wavefunction is evaluated at $\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{a}$ compared to $\mathbf{x}$.

$\\hbar$.name: Reduced Planck Constant
$\\hbar$.description: A fundamental physical constant that relates the energy of a photon to its frequency, and is central to quantum mechanics. It is equal to Planck's constant $h$ divided by $2\pi$.

$i$.name: Imaginary Unit
$i$.description: The imaginary unit, defined as the square root of -1. It is essential in quantum mechanics for describing phases and oscillations of wavefunctions.

$\\hat{\\mathbf{p}}$.name: Momentum Operator
$\\hat{\\mathbf{p}}$.description: The quantum mechanical operator corresponding to the linear momentum of a particle. In position representation, it is given by $\hat{\mathbf{p}} = -i\hbar \nabla$, where $\nabla$ is the gradient operator.

$\\mathbf{a} \\cdot \\hat{\\mathbf{p}}$.name: Scalar Product of Translation and Momentum Operator
$\\mathbf{a} \\cdot \\hat{\\mathbf{p}}$.description: The scalar product between the translation vector $\mathbf{a}$ and the momentum operator $\hat{\mathbf{p}}$. When this operator acts on the wavefunction, it effectively implements the spatial translation.

$p$.name: Linear Momentum ($p$)
$p$.description: The magnitude of linear momentum, representing the quantity of motion of a particle.

homogeneity-0c631165.interpretation: The equation $\psi(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{a}) = \exp($\frac{i}{\hbar}$\mathbf{a} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{p}} ) \psi(\mathbf{x})$ relates the wavefunction $\psi(\mathbf{x})$ of a quantum system at position $\mathbf{x}$ to its wavefunction $\psi(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{a})$ after it has been translated by a vector $\mathbf{a}$. The term $\exp($\frac{i}{\hbar}$\mathbf{a} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{p}} )$ is a unitary operator that represents this translation. Specifically, $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant, $i$ is the imaginary unit, $\mathbf{a}$ is the displacement vector (in meters), and $\hat{\mathbf{p}} = -i\hbar \nabla$ is the momentum operator. The dot product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{p}}$, when applied to the wavefunction, effectively translates the position dependence of the wavefunction. This formula is a direct consequence of the fact that the momentum operator is the generator of spatial translations. If the physical laws (and thus the Hamiltonian) are invariant under translation, this implies that momentum is conserved. The exponential form arises from the Taylor expansion of the translation operator, where $\hat{\mathbf{p}}/\hbar$ acts as the generator of translations.
homogeneity-0c631165.symmetry_origin: This formula originates from the fundamental principle of translational symmetry in physics. If the laws of physics governing a system do not depend on its absolute position in space, then the system exhibits translational symmetry. In quantum mechanics, symmetry transformations are represented by unitary operators. The generator of spatial translations is the momentum operator $\hat{\mathbf{p}}$. The relationship between a symmetry and its generator is mathematically formalized by the exponential form of the transformation operator, which in this case leads to the given formula.
homogeneity-0c631165.limits_and_boundary: As the translation vector $\mathbf{a}$ approaches zero (i.e., $\mathbf{a} \to \mathbf{0}$), the exponential term $\exp($\frac{i}{\hbar}$\mathbf{a} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{p}} )$ approaches $\exp(0) = 1$. This means $\psi(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{0}) = 1 \cdot \psi(\mathbf{x})$, which simplifies to $\psi(\mathbf{x}) = \psi(\mathbf{x})$. This is the expected result, as a zero translation should not change the wavefunction. Conversely, for very large translations $\mathbf{a}$ or very large momentum $\hat{\mathbf{p}}$, the phase factor oscillates rapidly, reflecting the wave-like nature of the quantum system and how its phase changes significantly with large displacements and momentum.
homogeneity-0c631165.conceptual_definition: This formula describes the transformation of a quantum mechanical wavefunction under a spatial translation. It states that if a system's Hamiltonian is invariant under translation (i.e., the laws of physics are the same everywhere in space), then its wavefunction must transform in a specific way when the spatial coordinates are shifted by a vector $\mathbf{a}$. This transformation is a phase factor that depends on the momentum operator, revealing a deep connection between translation symmetry and momentum conservation in quantum mechanics.
homogeneity-0c631165.intuitive_summary: Shifting a quantum system in space by $\mathbf{a}$ is equivalent to multiplying its wavefunction by a complex phase factor related to its momentum.

force-recovery-53d46087.title: Force Recovery

\\mathcal{L}.name: Lagrangian
\\mathcal{L}.description: The Lagrangian of the system, typically defined as the difference between the kinetic energy (T) and potential energy (V) of the system: $\mathcal{L} = T - V$. It is a function of generalized coordinates and their time derivatives.

q_i.name: Generalized Coordinate
q_i.description: The i-th generalized coordinate of the system. These are a set of independent variables that completely specify the configuration of the system. For example, angles or positions.

\\dot{q}_i.name: Generalized Velocity
\\dot{q}_i.description: The time derivative of the i-th generalized coordinate, representing the generalized velocity.

\\lambda.name: Lagrange Multiplier
\\lambda.description: A scalar multiplier used in the method of Lagrange multipliers to incorporate constraint forces into the equations of motion. It represents the magnitude of the generalized constraint force.

f.name: Constraint Function
f.description: A function that defines the constraint on the system's generalized coordinates. For a holonomic constraint, it is typically expressed in the form $f(q_1, q_2, ..., q_n) = 0$.

\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\partial.name: Generalized Force (from Lagrangian)
\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\partial.description: The generalized force component associated with the i-th coordinate, derived from the potential energy part of the Lagrangian (if $\mathcal{L} = T-V$ and $V$ depends on $q_i$). It represents the non-inertial force associated with the i-th degree of freedom.

\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\partial.name: Generalized Momentum
\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{L}}{\\partial.description: The i-th generalized momentum conjugate to the generalized coordinate $q_i$. It is defined as $p_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i}$.

\\frac{d}{dt}\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{.name: Rate of Change of Generalized Momentum
\\frac{d}{dt}\\frac{\\partial \\mathcal{.description: The time rate of change of the i-th generalized momentum. According to Newton's second law, this equals the net force in the generalized direction.

\\frac{\\partial f}{\\partial q_i}.name: Gradient of Constraint Function
\\frac{\\partial f}{\\partial q_i}.description: The partial derivative of the constraint function $f$ with respect to the generalized coordinate $q_i$. This term indicates how the constraint changes as $q_i$ changes, and it determines the direction of the constraint force.

$q$.name: Electric Charge
$q$.description: A physical property of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electromagnetic field.

$i$.name: Imaginary Unit
$i$.description: The mathematical constant defined by the property i² = -1 (sometimes written as j).

force-recovery-53d46087.interpretation: This equation is an extension of the Euler-Lagrange equations designed to handle systems with constraints. The term$\frac{d}{dt} \frac${\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} - $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i}$represents the generalized force acting on the system due to its inherent dynamics, derived from the Lagrangian$\mathcal{L}$. The Lagrangian itself is typically defined as the difference between kinetic energy$T$ and potential energy$V$ of the system,$\mathcal{L} = T - V$. The generalized coordinates are denoted by$q_i$, and their time derivatives (generalized velocities) by$\dot{q}_i$. The left-hand side essentially accounts for the forces that would exist if there were no constraints. The right-hand side,$\lambda$\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}$, represents the generalized constraint force. The function$f(q_1, q_2, ..., q_n) = 0$describes the constraint on the system's generalized coordinates. For example, a fixed length rod connecting two particles would impose a constraint. The Lagrange multiplier$\lambda$is a scalar that scales the constraint force. The term$\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}$is the gradient of the constraint function with respect to the generalized coordinate$q_i$, indicating the direction and magnitude of the constraint's influence on that coordinate. The entire right-hand side is the generalized component of the force arising from the constraint, which acts to ensure that$f$ remains zero.
force-recovery-53d46087.symmetry_origin: This formula originates from the principle of virtual work and D'Alembert's principle, which extends Newtonian mechanics into a more general variational framework. Specifically, it is derived from the Lagrangian formulation of mechanics when constraints are present. By applying the method of Lagrange multipliers to the variational principle, these equations emerge to ensure that the motion of the system is confined to the manifold defined by the constraint equations.
force-recovery-53d46087.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where there are no constraints (i.e.,$f$ is a constant or irrelevant, implying$\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i} = 0$ or$\lambda = 0$), the equation reduces to the standard Euler-Lagrange equation:$\frac{d}{dt} \frac${\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} - $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i}$ = 0$. This signifies that without constraints, the system's motion is solely governed by its Lagrangian. As$\lambda$approaches infinity (or a very large value), it implies that the constraint is very strong, and the constraint forces dominate the dynamics to rigidly enforce the condition$f=0$. Conversely, if$\lambda$ is zero, it indicates that the constraint imposes no force, which can happen if the constraint is holonomic and naturally satisfied by the system's degrees of freedom without external force, or if the gradient of the constraint is zero along the direction of motion.
force-recovery-53d46087.conceptual_definition: The given formula,$\frac{d}{dt} \frac${\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{q}_i} - $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial q_i}$ = \lambda $\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}$is a generalization of the Euler-Lagrange equations, incorporating constraint forces. The left side represents the generalized force associated with the system's dynamics derived from the Lagrangian$\mathcal{L}$. The right side introduces a Lagrange multiplier$\lambda$ and the gradient of a constraint function$f$, which together describe the force required to maintain the system within the specified constraints.
force-recovery-53d46087.intuitive_summary: This equation states that the inertial force associated with a system's generalized coordinates is balanced by the generalized constraint force, which is proportional to the gradient of the constraint function.

radial-action-b9aa9021.title: Radial Action

\\mathbf{F}_{12}.name: Force Vector
\\mathbf{F}_{12}.description: The vector representing the force exerted by object 1 on object 2. Its magnitude is measured in Newtons (N).

\\mathbf{r}_1.name: Position Vector of Object 1
\\mathbf{r}_1.description: The position vector of object 1 in a chosen coordinate system. Its SI unit is meters (m).

\\mathbf{r}_2.name: Position Vector of Object 2
\\mathbf{r}_2.description: The position vector of object 2 in a chosen coordinate system. Its SI unit is meters (m).

\\mathbf{r}_1 - \\mathbf{r}_2.name: Relative Position Vector
\\mathbf{r}_1 - \\mathbf{r}_2.description: The vector pointing from object 2 to object 1, representing their relative positions. Its SI unit is meters (m).

$F$.name: Force Magnitude
$F$.description: The magnitude of an interaction that causes an object with mass to accelerate.

$r$.name: Radial Distance / Radius
$r$.description: The radial distance from a central source or origin, typically used in spherical or cylindrical coordinate systems.

radial-action-b9aa9021.interpretation: In this equation, \mathbf{F}_{12} represents the force vector exerted by object 1 on object 2. The vector (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) is the position vector pointing from object 2 to object 1. The condition \parallel indicates that \mathbf{F}_{12} is parallel to (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) . This means that the force acts along the line segment joining the centers of the two objects. If \mathbf{F}_{12} is in the same direction as (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) , the force is repulsive. If it is in the opposite direction, the force is attractive. This property is characteristic of central forces, which are forces whose magnitude depends only on the distance between the two interacting bodies and whose direction is always along the line joining them.
radial-action-b9aa9021.symmetry_origin: This property of forces being radial, i.e., acting along the line connecting the centers of the interacting bodies, arises from fundamental symmetries, particularly rotational symmetry. If a force were not radial, applying a torque about the line connecting the centers would lead to angular acceleration, violating the principle of conservation of angular momentum for a system with no external torques. For instance, Newton's law of universal gravitation and Coulomb's law for electrostatic interaction are both central forces. The derivation often involves considering the potential energy function, which for central forces depends only on the radial separation, U(r) , where r = | \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2| .
radial-action-b9aa9021.limits_and_boundary: This formula describes the direction of the force at all separations. As the distance between the objects, r = | \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2| , approaches infinity, the magnitude of the force typically approaches zero (as seen in gravitational and electrostatic forces). As the distance approaches zero, the magnitude of the force generally increases, often unboundedly, unless other physical principles like the Pauli exclusion principle or structural integrity prevent objects from occupying the same space or interpenetrating significantly.
radial-action-b9aa9021.conceptual_definition: The formula \mathbf{F}_{12} \parallel (\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2) states that the force exerted by object 1 on object 2, denoted as \mathbf{F}_{12} , is always directed along the line connecting the positions of the two objects. The symbol \parallel signifies that the force vector is parallel to the vector representing the difference in their position vectors. This is a fundamental characteristic of many central forces in physics, such as gravitational and electrostatic forces.
radial-action-b9aa9021.intuitive_summary: The force between two objects acts directly along the straight line connecting them.

planck-cell-49fd3955.title: Planck Cell (The Wigner Quasi-Probability Distribution)

W(q, p).name: Wigner Quasi-Probability Distribution
W(q, p).description: The Wigner quasi-probability distribution is a function that represents a quantum mechanical state in phase space (position and momentum). While it shares some properties with classical probability distributions, it can take on negative values, hence 'quasi-probability'.

q.name: Position
q.description: The position coordinate of a particle in one-dimensional space. It represents the location of the particle.

p.name: Momentum
p.description: The momentum of a particle, defined as the product of its mass and velocity. It represents the particle's motion.

\\psi(q).name: Wavefunction
\\psi(q).description: The quantum mechanical wavefunction describing the state of a particle at a given position q. Its squared magnitude gives the probability density.

|\\psi(q)|^2.name: Position Probability Density
|\\psi(q)|^2.description: The probability density of finding the particle at position q. It is obtained by taking the squared magnitude of the wavefunction at that position.

dp.name: Differential Momentum Element
dp.description: An infinitesimal element of momentum, used in the integration process over all possible momentum values.

$W$.name: Electrostatic Energy
$W$.description: The potential energy stored in the electric field of a distribution of charges, or the total work required to assemble the charges.

planck-cell-49fd3955.interpretation: In this equation, $W(q, p)$ is the Wigner quasi-probability distribution, which provides a description of a quantum system in phase space, where $q represents position and$p represents momentum. The integral $\int W(q, p) \,$ dp signifies summing up the Wigner function's contributions across all possible momentum values for a fixed position $q$. The result of this integration, $|$\gamma$(q)|^2$, is the standard probability density of finding the particle at position $q$. Here, $\gamma$(q)$is the quantum mechanical wavefunction, and$|$\gamma$(q)|^2$is its squared magnitude, which is directly proportional to the probability of observing the particle at position$q$ in configuration space. This equation demonstrates that the marginal distribution in position obtained from the Wigner function is identical to the Born rule probability density.
planck-cell-49fd3955.symmetry_origin: This relation arises from the definition of the Wigner quasi-probability distribution and the properties of quantum mechanics. The Wigner function is constructed such that its marginals (integrations over position or momentum) yield the correct quantum mechanical probability distributions. This specific formula highlights the marginalization over momentum to recover the position probability density, a key aspect of its construction to bridge classical and quantum descriptions.
planck-cell-49fd3955.limits_and_boundary: As the range of integration for momentum approaches infinity (i.e., $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} W(q, p) \,$ dp), the equation holds true for any physically realistic, normalized wavefunction $\gamma$(q)$. If the Wigner function$W(q, p)$were to become zero for all momenta except within a very narrow range around some value$p_0$, then the integration would essentially pick out the value of$W(q, p_0)$(if$W$ is sufficiently well-behaved). However, the primary interpretation is the full integration over all momenta.
planck-cell-49fd3955.conceptual_definition: The Planck Cell formula, often encountered in the context of Wigner quasi-probability distributions, represents a fundamental relationship between the quantum mechanical wavefunction and its probability distribution in phase space. Specifically, this equation describes how integrating the Wigner function, a quasi-probability distribution in both position and momentum, over all possible momentum values yields the probability density of finding the particle at a given position.
planck-cell-49fd3955.intuitive_summary: Integrating the Wigner quasi-probability distribution over all momenta recovers the familiar probability density in position space.

transition-amplitude-f1086202.title: Transition Amplitude

S_{fi}.name: Transition Amplitude
S_{fi}.description: The complex-valued amplitude representing the probability of transitioning from an initial state |i, in> to a final state |f, out>.

|i, in\\rangle.name: Initial State (in-state)
|i, in\\rangle.description: The quantum state of the system prepared in the distant past (t -> -infinity), used as the starting point for a scattering process.

|f, out\\rangle.name: Final State (out-state)
|f, out\\rangle.description: The quantum state of the system observed in the distant future (t -> +infinity), used as the endpoint for a scattering process.

\\langle f, out | i, in \\rangle.name: Inner Product
\\langle f, out | i, in \\rangle.description: The scalar (complex) product of the bra vector representing the final state and the ket vector representing the initial state. This quantifies the overlap between the two states.

H.name: Hamiltonian
H.description: The operator representing the total energy of the quantum system, which governs its time evolution.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck Constant
\\hbar.description: A fundamental physical constant relating the energy of a photon to its frequency and the momentum of a particle to its wavelength. It appears in quantum mechanics to scale energy and time.

$S$.name: Poynting Vector
$S$.description: The directional energy flux density of an electromagnetic field.

$f$.name: Frequency
$f$.description: The number of occurrences of a repeating event per unit of time.

$o$.name: Origin / Offset
$o$.description: The starting point of a coordinate system, or baseline shift.

$u$.name: Velocity Component / Specific Internal Energy
$u$.description: Speed along a particular coordinate direction, or internal energy per unit mass.

$t$.name: Time
$t$.description: The continuous, progressive sequence of events in which change occurs. It acts as the independent variable in dynamical equations of motion.

$i$.name: Imaginary Unit
$i$.description: The mathematical constant defined by the property i² = -1 (sometimes written as j).

transition-amplitude-f1086202.interpretation: In the equation $S_{fi} = \langle f, out | i, in \rangle$, the symbol $S_{fi}$ represents the transition amplitude itself. The expression $\langle f, out | i, in \rangle$ is a Dirac notation, representing the inner product between the final state $|f, out\rangle$ and the initial state $|i, in\rangle$. The ket vector $|i, in\rangle$ denotes the initial state of the system as it is prepared in the distant past (time $t \to -\infty$), and the bra vector $\langle f, out |$ denotes the final state the system is observed in, as it would appear in the distant future (time $t \to +\infty$). The 'in' and 'out' labels are essential because, in interacting quantum systems, the states observed at asymptotic times are generally not the same as the states at finite times. The inner product $\langle f, out | i, in \rangle$ is a complex number whose magnitude squared, $|S_{fi}|^2$, gives the probability of observing the system in state $|f\rangle$ given that it started in state $|i\rangle$. This quantity encapsulates the entire dynamics of the interaction.
transition-amplitude-f1086202.symmetry_origin: The concept of transition amplitudes is deeply rooted in the time evolution of quantum states governed by the Schrödinger equation (or the Heisenberg equation for operators). For time-independent Hamiltonians, the time evolution operator is $U(t) = e^{-iHt/\hbar}$, where $H$ is the Hamiltonian and $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant. The transition amplitude can then be expressed as $S_{fi} = \lim_{t \to \infty, t' \to -\infty} \langle f | U(t, t') | i \rangle$, where $U(t, t')$ is the time-evolution operator between $t$' and $t$. In quantum field theory, the $S$-matrix (of which $S_{fi}$ is a matrix element) is often constructed using Feynman path integrals or diagrammatic methods (Feynman diagrams), which arise from the perturbative expansion of the time-evolution operator and reflect symmetries of the underlying Lagrangian.
transition-amplitude-f1086202.limits_and_boundary: In the absence of any interaction (i.e., if the Hamiltonian is such that the initial and final states are the same, or if the interaction is turned off), the transition amplitude for an initial state $|i\rangle$ to transition to itself would be $S_{ii} = 1$ (representing a probability of 1), and for transitions to different states $|f\rangle eq |i\rangle$, $S_{fi} = 0$. transition-amplitude-f1086202.conceptual_definition: The Transition Amplitude, denoted by $S_{fi} = \langle f, out | i, in \rangle$, is a fundamental quantity in quantum mechanics and quantum field theory that quantifies the probability amplitude for a quantum system to transition from an initial state $|i, in\rangle$ to a final state $|f, out\rangle$. It is a complex number whose squared magnitude, $|S_{fi}|^2$, gives the probability of this transition. The 'in' and 'out' labels refer to states defined at asymptotic times, meaning far in the past (initial state) and far in the future (final state), respectively. This concept is crucial for understanding scattering processes, particle decays, and other dynamical evolutions of quantum systems.
transition-amplitude-f1086202.intuitive_summary: The transition amplitude measures the likelihood that a quantum system starting in a specific initial state will end up in a specific final state after evolving over time.

The sum is taken over a complete orthonormal basis, denoted by the set of kets $codemath$|n>$/`math/code$. vector-expansion-a9fb4aba.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the fundamental postulates of quantum mechanics, specifically the existence of a Hilbert space to represent quantum states and the concept of a complete orthonormal basis. vector-expansion-a9fb4aba.conceptual_definition: The formula $codemath$\hat{ I } = \sum{ n } |n>< n|$/`math/code$ represents the identity operator in quantum mechanics. vector-expansion-a9fb4aba.intuitive_summary: Any quantum state can be perfectly represented by summing up its projections onto a complete set of basis states.

contraction-b554a42d.interpretation: The formula describes the scalar product of two four-vectors, $A$ and $B$. The expression $A eq B$ is not precise, but the contraction is mathematically represented as $A^ u B_ u$ or $A_ u B^ u$. The sum is over the repeated index $u$, which runs from 0 to 3 (0 for time, 1, 2, 3 for spatial dimensions). The relationship between contravariant and covariant components is given by the metric tensor, $A_ u = \tensor{g}{ u\rho} A^\rho$ and $A^ u = \tensor{g}{ u\rho} A_\rho$, where $\tensor{g}{ u\rho}$ is the metric tensor of spacetime. The result of the contraction, $A^ u B_ u$, is a scalar quantity, meaning it has the same value for all inertial observers in special relativity, and for all observers in general relativity under appropriate conditions of coordinate invariance. The term 'inv' likely stands for 'invariant'. For instance, if $A$ represents the four-momentum of a particle and $B$ represents its four-velocity, their contraction yields the square of the rest mass of the particle, a fundamental invariant.
contraction-b554a42d.symmetry_origin: The contraction of four-vectors is rooted in the principle of Lorentz invariance in special relativity and the principle of general covariance in general relativity. The scalar result ensures that physical laws expressed using this contraction remain consistent across different inertial frames (special relativity) or any coordinate system (general relativity), reflecting a deep symmetry of spacetime.
contraction-b554a42d.limits_and_boundary: The contraction operation itself does not typically have simple limits as individual components of the vectors approach zero or infinity in a universal way, as the result depends on the specific nature and components of the vectors $A$ and $B$. contraction-b554a42d.conceptual_definition: The contraction of two four-vectors, denoted by A and B, in spacetime is a fundamental operation in special and general relativity. It results in a scalar quantity, meaning it is invariant under Lorentz transformations (in special relativity) or more general coordinate transformations (in general relativity). This scalar is represented by the dot product in Minkowski spacetime, where one vector is raised in index and the other is lowered using the metric tensor.
contraction-b554a42d.intuitive_summary: The contraction of two spacetime vectors yields a scalar invariant, representing a projection-like interaction between them that is independent of the observer's reference frame.

nuclear-equilibrium-8893b2a8.interpretation: The formula, $n_i \approx g_i \left($\frac{m_i kT}{2\pi \hbar^2}$\right)^{3/2} e^{(\mu_i - m_ic^2)/kT}$, expresses the number density $n_i$ (particles per cubic meter, m⁻³) of a particular species of particle $i$. The term $g_i$ represents the degeneracy factor, accounting for any internal quantum states or spin states that are energetically equivalent. The quantity $k$ is the Boltzmann constant (J/K), which relates temperature to energy, and $T$ is the absolute temperature (K). The term $m_i$ is the rest mass of the particle $i$ (kg), and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum (m/s). $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant (J·s), a fundamental constant in quantum mechanics. The exponential term $e^{(\mu_i - m_ic^2)/kT}$ is crucial: $\mu_i$ is the chemical potential (J) for particle species $i$, which governs the particle flow between different states or systems to maintain equilibrium. $m_ic^2$ represents the rest mass energy of the particle, a key component in relativistic considerations. The ratio $(\mu_i - m_ic^2)/kT$ indicates how readily particles occupy states relative to their rest mass energy, modulated by thermal energy $kT$. The term $\left($\frac{m_i kT}{2\pi \hbar^2}$\right)^{3/2}$ is related to the thermal de Broglie wavelength, representing the density of accessible quantum states per unit volume.
nuclear-equilibrium-8893b2a8.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from statistical mechanics, specifically from the principles of quantum statistics (e.g., Bose-Einstein or Fermi-Dirac statistics, though the form presented resembles a high-temperature or dilute-gas approximation of Maxwell-Boltzmann statistics). It is a consequence of maximizing the entropy of the system subject to constraints on the total number of particles and total energy, leading to the Lagrange multiplier method which introduces the chemical potential $\mu_i$. The quantum nature is introduced via the density of states, which is related to Planck's constant $\hbar$. The formula is invariant under translations and rotations because density is a scalar quantity and the system is assumed to be homogeneous and isotropic.
nuclear-equilibrium-8893b2a8.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the rest mass energy $m_ic^2$ is much larger than the thermal energy $kT$ and the chemical potential $\mu_i$, and when the particle density is low, the exponential term $e^{(\mu_i - m_ic^2)/kT}$ becomes very small, indicating a low probability of particle formation or occupation of states. Conversely, as $kT$ increases relative to $m_ic^2$, or as $\mu_i$ approaches $m_ic^2$, the exponential term increases, leading to higher particle densities. If $\mu_i - m_ic^2$ were to become significantly positive and large, it would imply an unphysically high density of particles or energy, suggesting the formula's applicability limits are being exceeded, or that the system is not in equilibrium. The factor $\left($\frac{m_i kT}{2\pi \hbar^2}$\right)^{3/2}$ shows that at higher temperatures or lower masses, the density of accessible quantum states increases, favoring higher particle densities.
nuclear-equilibrium-8893b2a8.conceptual_definition: The provided formula, known as the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution for non-relativistic particles in a relativistic context, or more generally, the distribution function for particles in thermal equilibrium, describes the average number density of particles of a specific type, denoted by the subscript $i$, in a system that has reached thermal equilibrium. It relates this number density to fundamental thermodynamic quantities like temperature and chemical potential, as well as particle-specific properties such as mass and degeneracy, and quantum mechanical parameters like Planck's constant.
nuclear-equilibrium-8893b2a8.intuitive_summary: This equation quantifies how many particles of a certain type are expected to be found in a system at thermal equilibrium, considering their mass, available energy states, temperature, and the tendency to minimize energy.

ρₑₘ.description: The average density of dark matter over the observable universe. This is not directly measured but inferred from its gravitational effects.

cosmological-density-32ad3381.interpretation: In the context of modern cosmology, the universe's geometry and its ultimate fate are determined by its total energy density. The critical density, ρ$\mathbf{k}$, is the specific density that would result in a spatially flat universe. The actual average density of the universe is composed of several components, including ordinary baryonic matter, dark matter (ρ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ), radiation, and dark energy. The cosmological density parameter for dark matter, Θ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ, is defined as the ratio of the average density of dark matter (ρ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ) to the critical density (ρ$\mathbf{k}$): Θ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ = ρ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ / ρ$\mathbf{k}$. The value Θ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ ≈ 0.27 indicates that dark matter accounts for approximately 27% of the critical density. This value is derived from various cosmological observations, such as the cosmic microwave background radiation, large-scale structure surveys, and gravitational lensing.
cosmological-density-32ad3381.symmetry_origin: The concept of cosmological density parameters arises from the Friedmann equations, which are derived from Einstein's field equations of general relativity applied to a homogeneous and isotropic universe. The critical density is a consequence of balancing the expansion of the universe (driven by its energy density) against the gravitational attraction that would slow it down. The critical density itself is dependent on the Hubble constant, Η₀, which characterizes the current expansion rate of the universe. The invariance to coordinate transformations inherent in general relativity is foundational to these equations.
cosmological-density-32ad3381.limits_and_boundary: The value of Θ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ is a specific, measured parameter of our current universe and does not typically approach limits of zero or infinity in a theoretical sense within this equation. However, if one were to consider hypothetical universes with significantly different amounts of dark matter, Θ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ could conceptually be very small (approaching 0) in a universe dominated by other forms of energy, or potentially larger if dark matter were the overwhelmingly dominant component. The total cosmological density parameter, Θ$\mathbf{k}$ᴜᴜᴐᴓᴐₗ, which is the sum of density parameters for all components (Θ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ + Θᴗᴐᴐᴐᴐ + Θᴑᴐᴐᴐᴓᴐᴐᴐ + Θᴑᴐᴐᴐᴐᴐᴐᴐᴐᴐᴐᴐ), is expected to be close to 1 for a flat universe.
cosmological-density-32ad3381.conceptual_definition: The cosmological density parameter, denoted by Θ, represents the ratio of the actual average density of matter and energy in the universe to the critical density required for a flat universe. The equation Θ$\mathbf{R}$ₘ ≈ 0.27 specifically refers to the contribution of dark matter to this total cosmological density.
cosmological-density-32ad3381.intuitive_summary: Dark matter constitutes about 27% of the total cosmic density needed for a flat universe.

definition-4efeafdf.title: Definition (General Relativistic Singularity Theory)

definition-4efeafdf.interpretation: The equation R_{$\mu u\rho\sigma}R^{\mu u\rho\sigma} \rightarrow \infty$ involves the Riemann curvature tensor, denoted as $R_{\mu u\rho\sigma}$. definition-4efeafdf.symmetry_origin: The Riemann curvature tensor and its invariants are fundamental to General Relativity because they are coordinate-independent (scalar) quantities that describe the intrinsic curvature of spacetime, independent of the observer's frame of reference. definition-4efeafdf.limits_and_boundary: As one approaches a singularity, the Kretschmann scalar $R_{\mu u\rho\sigma}R^{\mu u\rho\sigma}$ diverges to positive infinity. definition-4efeafdf.conceptual_definition: This equation, relating to General Relativistic Singularity Theory, describes a condition where the curvature of spacetime becomes infinitely large. In General Relativity, gravity is understood as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. A singularity represents a point or region where the known laws of physics break down, typically characterized by infinite density and spacetime curvature. The expression shown is the scalar invariant known as the Kretschmann scalar, which is a measure of the magnitude of the Riemann curvature tensor. geometric-duality-8302add6.interpretation: In this equation, R_{T} represents the radius of the compactified dimension in the dual theory, while R represents the radius of the compactified dimension in the original theory. geometric-duality-8302add6.symmetry_origin: Geometric duality (T-duality) arises from the symmetries inherent in the worldsheet theory of strings. This limit suggests that a theory with a very small compactification radius is equivalent to a theory with a large compactification radius in its dual description. These limits highlight how T-duality can relate theories in regimes of vastly different geometric scales.
geometric-duality-8302add6.conceptual_definition: Geometric duality, also known as T-duality (or target space duality), is a profound symmetry in string theory and M-theory that relates two different string theories or different compactifications of the same theory, which appear geometrically distinct but are physically equivalent. Specifically, it states that a string theory compactified on a circle of radius R is equivalent to another string theory compactified on a circle of radius 1/R, where 1 is a characteristic length scale of the theory. The formula provided, R_{T} = 1^2/R, is a specific instance of this duality, relating the radius of the compactified space in one theory to that in the dual theory. This implies that large radii in one description correspond to small radii in the dual description, and vice-versa.
geometric-duality-8302add6.intuitive_summary: Large circles in one string theory correspond to small circles in a physically identical, but geometrically different, string theory.

action-variation-endpoints-7836a821.title: Variation of Action (Endpoint Identity)
action-variation-endpoints-7836a821.interpretation: The formula ΔS = [$\sum$_i p_i Δq_i - H Δt]_{t_1}^{t_2} represents the change in the action, S, of a physical system. action-variation-endpoints-7836a821.symmetry_origin: This formula is a direct consequence of Hamilton's principle of stationary action. Hamilton's principle is deeply connected to the time translation symmetry of the Lagrangian. If the Lagrangian is invariant under time translations (i.e., it does not explicitly depend on time, ∂L/∂t = 0), then the Hamiltonian (which is related to the total energy) is conserved. The variation of the action being zero for fixed endpoints implies the conservation of this quantity. The derivation typically involves varying the path of integration in the action integral and applying integration by parts, leading to the equations of motion and the boundary terms given.
action-variation-endpoints-7836a821.limits_and_boundary: When the variation in time Δt approaches zero, and the variations in position Δq_i at the endpoints also approach zero (as in the endpoint identity condition), the entire expression [$\sum$_i p_i Δq_i - H Δt]_{t_1}^{t_2} becomes zero. This implies that for a system starting and ending at the same position at the same time, the action is stationary. If the endpoints are not fixed, the non-zero values of the bracketed term at the boundaries contribute to the total variation of the action, providing information about how the action changes with respect to changes in the endpoint positions and times.

action-variation-endpoints-7836a821.conceptual_definition: The formula for the variation of the action, specifically when the endpoints of the path are held fixed in position, is a fundamental result derived from Hamilton's principle. Hamilton's principle states that the path taken by a physical system between two points in configuration space and time is the one for which the action is stationary. The variation of the action, ΔS, quantifies how the action changes for infinitesimal deviations from this true path. The presented form of ΔS = [$\sum$_i p_i Δq_i - H Δt]_{t_1}^{t_2} specifically addresses the case where the variation in time and the generalized coordinates at the initial and final times are zero, i.e., Δq_i(t_1) = Δq_i(t_2) = 0 and Δt = 0. This condition leads to the principle of least action, which asserts that ΔS = 0 for the actual physical path.
action-variation-endpoints-7836a821.intuitive_summary: The variation in the action is zero for a physical path if the starting and ending positions and times are fixed, reflecting the path of least 'effort' or change.

electroweak-covariant-derivative-full-19.title: Electroweak Covariant Derivative
electroweak-covariant-derivative-full-19.equation: D_\mu = \partial_\mu - i g \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{W}_\mu - i g' \frac{Y}{2} B_\mu
electroweak-covariant-derivative-full-19.interpretation: The Electroweak Covariant Derivative$D_\mu$is composed of three terms. The first term, ∂₂ , is the standard partial derivative with respect to spacetime coordinate$x^\mu$. This term accounts for the intrinsic change in a field as one moves through spacetime, independent of interactions. The second term,$-i g \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{W}_\mu$, describes the interaction with the weak isospin gauge fields. Here,$g$is the coupling constant for the weak interaction,$∂$represents the Pauli matrices acting as generators of the SU(2) gauge group, and$∂$is a vector of the three W bosons ($W^1_\mu, W^2_\mu, W^3_\mu$). This term couples fermions (which carry weak isospin) to the W bosons. The third term,$-i g'$\frac{Y}{2}$B_\mu$, describes the interaction with the hypercharge gauge field$B_\mu$.$g$' is the coupling constant for the hypercharge interaction,$Y$is the hypercharge of the particle, and$B_\mu$is the gauge field associated with hypercharge. This term couples particles to the B boson. Together, these terms ensure that the Lagrangian remains invariant under local electroweak gauge transformations, which involves independent transformations at each point in spacetime.
electroweak-covariant-derivative-full-19.symmetry_origin: The Electroweak Covariant Derivative arises from the principle of gauge invariance in the Standard Model. Specifically, it is derived from requiring that the Lagrangian describing fermions and bosons remains invariant under local SU(2) × U(1) gauge transformations. This requirement forces the introduction of gauge fields ($∂$and$B_\mu$) and dictates the form of their interactions with fermions, as encapsulated by the covariant derivative.
electroweak-covariant-derivative-full-19.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the coupling constants$g$and$g$' approach zero, the electroweak covariant derivative reduces to the ordinary partial derivative ∂₂ . This scenario corresponds to a situation with no electroweak interactions, where fields evolve independently. In the context of symmetry breaking, the electroweak symmetry is spontaneously broken, leading to the massive W and Z bosons and the photon. The covariant derivative in its full form is used for the unbroken symmetry phase and is essential for understanding the interactions in the early universe or at very high energy scales before symmetry breaking becomes significant. The specific combinations of fields that become massive (W±, Z) and massless (photon) are derived from the gauge fields$∂$and$B_\mu$, and the covariant derivative is fundamental to this process.

D_μ.description: The spacetime derivative operator that is invariant under local electroweak gauge transformations. Its units are inverse length, consistent with a derivative.

The unit of a gauge field is typically energy or momentum per unit charge, which can be represented here in base SI units if considering force context, or more abstractly as having units that make the covariant derivative dimensionally correct. Given other terms, it effectively carries units of (energy)/(charge) or equivalent for interaction terms.

Similar to W_μ, its units are related to energy/charge.

$D$.name: Electric Displacement Field
$D$.description: The displacement flux density representing electric charge polarization in media.

$W$.name: Electrostatic Energy

$B$.name: Magnetic Field Strength
$B$.description: The magnetic flux density representing electromagnetic field induction.

electroweak-covariant-derivative-full-19.conceptual_definition: The Electroweak Covariant Derivative, denoted as$D_\mu = \partial_\mu - i g \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{W}_\mu - i g'$\frac{Y}{2}$B_\mu$is a fundamental operator in the Standard Model of particle physics. It is a generalization of the ordinary partial derivative ( ∂₂ ) that correctly describes how fields transform under gauge transformations, particularly in the context of electroweak interactions. It ensures that physical laws remain invariant under local gauge transformations, which is a cornerstone of quantum field theory. The covariant derivative is essential for constructing the kinetic terms of gauge bosons and fermions in a gauge-invariant manner, incorporating the interactions between these particles.
electroweak-covariant-derivative-full-19.intuitive_summary: It's a modified derivative that accounts for the interactions of particles with the fundamental force fields of the electroweak force.

page-time-entanglement-1de816de.interpretation: $S_R$ is the entanglement entropy of the Hawking radiation, and $S_{BH}$ is the thermodynamic entropy of the black hole.
page-time-entanglement-1de816de.symmetry_origin: Unitary quantum evolution of black hole evaporation.
page-time-entanglement-1de816de.limits_and_boundary: Before the Page time, the entanglement entropy rises linearly. After the Page time, the entanglement entropy decreases to zero as the black hole evaporates completely.

page-time-entanglement-1de816de.conceptual_definition: In black hole thermodynamics and quantum information, the Page Time Entanglement Inequality describes the behavior of the entanglement entropy $S_R$ of Hawking radiation. After the Page time, the entanglement entropy of the radiation must start to decrease and track the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of the remaining black hole to preserve quantum unitarity.
page-time-entanglement-1de816de.intuitive_summary: To avoid violating quantum information conservation, the entanglement entropy of particles escaping a black hole must decrease in the second half of its lifetime, tracking the remaining black hole entropy.

four-potential-components.title: Four-potential components
four-potential-components.conceptual_definition: The four-potential is a fundamental object in relativistic electrodynamics, combining the scalar electric potential and the vector magnetic potential into a single four-vector. This formulation elegantly unifies electric and magnetic fields and simplifies the expression of electromagnetic phenomena in the framework of special relativity.
four-potential-components.intuitive_summary: The four-potential is a relativistic construct that elegantly merges the scalar electric potential and the vector magnetic potential into a single entity, simplifying the description of electromagnetic fields.
four-potential-components.interpretation: The equation defines the four-potential, denoted as a four-vector $A_\mu$. In the context of special relativity, spacetime coordinates are often represented by $x^\mu = (ct, x, y, z)$, where $c$ is the speed of light and $t$ is time. The four-potential $A_\mu$ is a four-vector whose components are intrinsically linked to electromagnetic fields. The first component, $A_0$, is related to the scalar electric potential $\Phi$ by $A_0 = -\Phi/c$. This component carries units of electric potential divided by velocity, resulting in units of electric flux density (or magnetic field strength, Wb/m^2), which is equivalent to Tesla-meter in SI units, or kg/(A*s^2) in base SI units. The remaining components, $A_1, A_2, A_3$, form the three-dimensional vector magnetic potential, denoted as $\mathbf{A}$. These components correspond to the $x, y, z$ directions of the magnetic potential, which has units of magnetic flux per unit length (Weber per meter, Wb/m), equivalent to Tesla-meter in SI units, or kg/(A*s) in base SI units. The relationship between the four-potential and the electromagnetic fields (represented by the electromagnetic field tensor $F_{\mu u}$) is given by $F_{\mu u} = \partial_\mu A_ u - \partial_ u A_\mu$. This implies that the scalar electric potential and vector magnetic potential are not independent but are components of a unified relativistic field.
four-potential-components.symmetry_origin: The origin of the four-potential formulation lies in the requirement of Lorentz invariance for the laws of electromagnetism. Maxwell's equations are not explicitly Lorentz covariant when expressed in terms of scalar and vector potentials separately. By combining them into a four-vector, the electromagnetic potentials become components of a single object that transforms correctly under Lorentz transformations, ensuring that the physics of electromagnetism remains the same for all inertial observers.
four-potential-components.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit, where velocities are much smaller than the speed of light ($v \ll c$), the magnetic effects become negligible. In this limit, the vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ approaches zero, and the dynamics are primarily governed by the scalar electric potential $\Phi$. As the speed of light $c$ approaches infinity (a hypothetical scenario not physically realized), the relationship between the scalar potential component $A_0$ and $\Phi$ would change, potentially leading to a separation of electric and magnetic phenomena.

A_\\mu.description: The four-potential is a four-vector in spacetime that encapsulates both the scalar electric potential and the vector magnetic potential. Its components are $A_0 = -\Phi/c$, and $A_i$ for $i=1, 2, 3$ which form the vector potential $\mathbf{A}$.

\\Phi.name: Scalar Electric Potential
\\Phi.description: The scalar electric potential is the electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in space. It is the source of the electric field in the absence of changing magnetic fields.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum

\\mathbf{A}.name: Vector Magnetic Potential
\\mathbf{A}.description: The vector magnetic potential is a vector field whose curl gives the magnetic field. It is related to the magnetic field in a similar way that the electric field is related to the scalar electric potential.

density-profile.title: Density Profile
density-profile.conceptual_definition: The formula $\rho(r)$ = c_s^2 / (2̂ G r^2) describes the radial density profile of a self-gravitating, spherically symmetric system in hydrostatic equilibrium, particularly relevant in astrophysics for phenomena like accretion disks or the density distribution within certain stellar models. It posits that the density $\rho(r) at a radial distance r$ from the center decreases quadratically with r, influenced by the sound speed c_s and the gravitational constant G.
density-profile.intuitive_summary: In a spherically symmetric, self-gravitating system in equilibrium, the density decreases rapidly with distance from the center, inversely proportional to the square of the radius.
density-profile.interpretation: This equation relates the density of a medium, $\rho(r)$, at a distance r from the center of a spherically symmetric, self-gravitating object to fundamental physical quantities. The term c_s represents the sound speed within the medium, which is a measure of the internal pressure support against gravitational collapse. A higher sound speed implies greater pressure support, which, according to this formula, would lead to a higher density at any given radius. The term G is the universal gravitational constant, indicating the strength of gravity. The inverse square dependence on the radius, 1/r^2, signifies that the density drops off sharply as one moves away from the center. This relationship is derived under the assumption of hydrostatic equilibrium, where the inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure gradient, and also typically assumes spherical symmetry and a specific equation of state for the medium.
density-profile.symmetry_origin: The derivation of this density profile typically originates from the equations of hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry in gravitational systems. Specifically, it arises from balancing the pressure gradient force, which pushes outward, against the gravitational force, which pulls inward. For a spherically symmetric mass distribution, the gravitational force at radius r is determined by the mass enclosed within that radius. When considering a medium with a sound speed c_s (related to pressure) and assuming it is in equilibrium under its own gravity, this specific form of density dependence with radius emerges, particularly in contexts like thin accretion disks or certain degenerate matter configurations.
density-profile.limits_and_boundary: As the radial distance r approaches zero (r → 0), the density $\rho(r)$ approaches infinity ($\gamma$̒). This indicates that for this model to hold, the central density would be infinitely large, which is a physical singularity and suggests that the model breaks down at the very center or that a different physical regime dominates. As the radial distance r approaches infinity (r → ∞), the density $\rho(r)$ approaches zero ($\gamma$̒). This implies that the density of the medium vanishes far from the central source, as expected in most astrophysical contexts.

\\rho(r).name: Density Profile
\\rho(r).description: The density of the medium as a function of the radial distance r from the center of the system.

c_s.name: Sound Speed
c_s.description: The speed of sound within the medium. It is related to the internal pressure and is a measure of the medium's resistance to compression and its ability to support itself against gravitational collapse.

G.name: Gravitational Constant
G.description: The universal gravitational constant, which quantifies the strength of the gravitational attraction between masses.

r.name: Radial Distance
r.description: The distance from the center of the spherically symmetric system to the point where the density is being evaluated.

gravitational-redshift.title: Gravitational Redshift
gravitational-redshift.conceptual_definition: The Gravitational Redshift formula quantifies the fractional change in frequency (or wavelength) of light as it travels out of a gravitational potential well. Specifically, it describes how light loses energy when escaping a massive object, causing its frequency to decrease and its wavelength to increase, shifting towards the red end of the electromagnetic spectrum. This phenomenon is a direct consequence of Einstein's theory of General Relativity.
gravitational-redshift.intuitive_summary: Light loses energy as it climbs out of a gravity well, causing its wavelength to stretch.
gravitational-redshift.interpretation: The gravitational redshift, denoted by the dimensionless quantity $z_g$, is given by the ratio $z_g = G M / (R c^2)$. Here, $G$ is the universal gravitational constant, representing the fundamental strength of gravitational attraction between masses. $M$ is the mass of the celestial object from which the light is escaping, as a larger mass creates a deeper gravitational potential. $R$ is the radial distance from the center of the massive object to the point where the light is emitted or observed (often taken as the radius of the object if observed from its surface). $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum, a fundamental constant of nature. The equation shows that the redshift is directly proportional to the gravitational potential at the emission point (represented by the product $GM/R$) and inversely proportional to the square of the speed of light. A larger product $GM/R$ leads to a greater redshift, indicating that light loses more energy escaping from a more massive or denser object. The $c^2$ term in the denominator acts as a conversion factor, relating gravitational potential energy to relativistic energy.
gravitational-redshift.symmetry_origin: Gravitational redshift is a relativistic effect predicted by Einstein's field equations of General Relativity. It arises from the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. In a gravitational field, spacetime is not flat, and the path of light (and indeed all objects) is affected. When light escapes a gravitational potential, it does work against the gravitational field, losing energy. This energy loss manifests as a decrease in frequency and an increase in wavelength. The formula can be derived from the Schwarzschild metric for a static, spherically symmetric gravitational field, considering the trajectory of photons. It can also be understood as a consequence of the equivalence principle, which relates gravity to acceleration, and thus to the changing gravitational potential experienced by the light as it propagates.
gravitational-redshift.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of a very weak gravitational field, where $GM/(Rc^2) \to 0$ (i.e., for objects with very small mass $M$ or observed from very large distances $R$, such that the gravitational potential is negligible compared to $c^2$), the gravitational redshift $z_g$ approaches zero. This corresponds to the classical physics regime where light frequency is unaffected by gravity. In the opposite limit, approaching the event horizon of a black hole ($R \to 2GM/c^2$, the Schwarzschild radius), the denominator of the expression $GM/(Rc^2)$ approaches $c^2/2$. While the formula derived for weak fields is an approximation, it suggests that the redshift would become very large as $R$ approaches the Schwarzschild radius, tending towards infinity at the event horizon itself. This indicates that light emitted from near a black hole's event horizon would be severely redshifted, to the point of becoming undetectable.

z_g.name: Gravitational Redshift
z_g.description: The dimensionless fractional change in frequency of light due to gravity. A positive value indicates a redshift (frequency decrease, wavelength increase).

G.description: The universal gravitational constant, which determines the strength of the gravitational force between two masses.

M.description: The mass of the celestial object creating the gravitational field from which the light is escaping.

c.description: The speed of light in a vacuum, a fundamental physical constant.

transformation-normal-coordinates.title: Transformation to Normal Coordinates
transformation-normal-coordinates.conceptual_definition: The equation$\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{U} \boldsymbol{\eta}$represents a linear transformation from a set of normal coordinates ($\boldsymbol{\eta}$) to a set of generalized coordinates ($\mathbf{x}$). Normal coordinates are a special set of generalized coordinates that decouple the equations of motion, typically in systems with multiple degrees of freedom exhibiting harmonic oscillations or vibrations. The matrix$\mathbf{U}$serves as the transformation matrix that maps the normal coordinates to the generalized coordinates.
transformation-normal-coordinates.intuitive_summary: This formula transforms a set of decoupled, fundamental modes of oscillation (normal coordinates) into the coupled, observable positions or generalized coordinates of a system.
transformation-normal-coordinates.interpretation: In this formula,$\mathbf{x}$represents a vector of generalized coordinates describing the configuration of a physical system. These coordinates can be positions, angles, or other variables that define the state of the system. The vector$\boldsymbol{\eta}$represents a set of normal coordinates. These are a special choice of coordinates such that the system's equations of motion become simple harmonic oscillators that do not interact with each other. The matrix$\mathbf{U}$is the transformation matrix that relates these two sets of coordinates. It is often derived from the system's mass and stiffness matrices and its eigenvectors. Specifically, if a system's kinetic and potential energies are written in terms of generalized coordinates, a suitable transformation can be found such that these energies are diagonal in the normal coordinates, simplifying the dynamics.
transformation-normal-coordinates.symmetry_origin: The origin of this transformation lies in the desire to simplify the dynamics of systems with multiple degrees of freedom, particularly those exhibiting small oscillations around an equilibrium point. For such systems, the equations of motion are linear and can be expressed in matrix form. The process of finding normal coordinates and the associated transformation matrix$\mathbf{U}$involves diagonalizing the system's dynamical matrix, which is related to the mass and stiffness properties of the system. This diagonalization effectively decouples the equations of motion, revealing the independent modes of vibration (normal modes) and their characteristic frequencies. The transformation is fundamentally linked to the symmetry properties of the system and its potential energy.
transformation-normal-coordinates.limits_and_boundary: As$\boldsymbol{\eta}$approaches the zero vector,$\mathbf{x}$also approaches the zero vector, indicating that when all normal modes are at rest, the system is at its equilibrium configuration. If the elements of$\boldsymbol{\eta}$approach infinity, the elements of$\mathbf{x}$will also approach infinity, scaled by the elements of$\mathbf{U}$. In the context of oscillations, this implies that very large amplitudes in the normal modes correspond to very large amplitudes in the generalized coordinates, with the amplitudes dictated by the transformation matrix.

\\mathbf{x}.name: Generalized Coordinates Vector
\\mathbf{x}.description: A column vector representing the generalized coordinates of the system, which describe its configuration. For example, these could be positions, angles, or displacements from an equilibrium.

\\mathbf{U}.name: Transformation Matrix
\\mathbf{U}.description: A matrix that transforms the normal coordinates into the generalized coordinates. The columns of this matrix typically represent the eigenvectors of the system's dynamical matrix, which correspond to the normal modes of vibration.

\\boldsymbol{\\eta}.name: Normal Coordinates Vector
\\boldsymbol{\\eta}.description: A column vector representing the normal coordinates of the system. These are a set of coordinates that decouple the equations of motion, such that each normal coordinate oscillates independently as a simple harmonic oscillator.

yield-parameter.title: Yield Parameter
yield-parameter.conceptual_definition: The Yield Parameter, represented by the formula $Y = n/s$, quantifies the efficiency or output of a process relative to some measure of input or scale. It is a dimensionless quantity that indicates how effectively a given resource or capacity is utilized to produce a desired outcome.
yield-parameter.intuitive_summary: The Yield Parameter tells you how much output you get per unit of input or scale.
yield-parameter.interpretation: In the formula $Y = n/s$, $Y$ is the Yield Parameter. The variable $n$ represents the 'numerator' quantity, which is typically the measure of the result, output, or favorable events. The variable $s$ represents the 'denominator' quantity, which serves as the scale, total number of opportunities, or input resource. The division of $n$ by $s$ normalizes the output $n$ by the extent of the operation or system $s$, providing a standardized measure of performance or yield. For instance, if $n$ is the number of successful products manufactured and $s$ is the total number of attempted manufacturing cycles, $Y$ would represent the success rate per cycle. Conversely, if $n$ is the amount of useful energy extracted and $s$ is the total energy input, $Y$ would represent the energy efficiency.
yield-parameter.symmetry_origin: The origin of this formula is purely definitional, arising from the need to normalize a quantity of interest (the 'numerator') by a relevant measure of scale or effort (the 'denominator') to obtain a meaningful ratio or efficiency metric. It does not stem from a fundamental conservation law or symmetry principle but rather from practical empirical or statistical analysis.
yield-parameter.limits_and_boundary: As $s$ approaches infinity (for a fixed, finite $n$), the Yield Parameter $Y$ approaches 0. This signifies that with an infinitely large scale or input, the relative contribution of a fixed output becomes negligible. As $n$ approaches 0 (for a fixed, finite $s$), the Yield Parameter $Y$ also approaches 0, indicating no yield or output. If both $n$ and $s$ approach 0, the limit of $Y$ depends on the specific relationship between $n$ and $s$ (e.g., if $n =$ ks, then $Y = k$). If $n$ is much larger than $s$, $Y$ will be greater than 1, indicating a yield that exceeds the scale, which might imply that the 'scale' itself is not the limiting factor or that $n$ represents something other than a direct count within the scope of $s$.

Y.name: Yield Parameter
Y.description: The dimensionless parameter representing the ratio of a quantity of interest to a measure of scale or input.

n.name: Numerator Quantity
n.description: The quantity representing the output, successful events, or desired outcome. Its SI units depend on the specific physical context.

s.name: Scale or Denominator Quantity
s.description: The quantity representing the total scale, input, effort, or opportunities. Its SI units depend on the specific physical context and must be commensurate with the units of n for Y to be dimensionless if n and s have the same units.

higgs-lagrangian.title: Higgs Lagrangian
higgs-lagrangian.conceptual_definition: The Higgs Lagrangian, denoted as ℓ_{\text{Higgs}}, is a fundamental component of the Standard Model of particle physics. It describes the behavior and interactions of the Higgs field, a scalar field that permeates the universe. This Lagrangian is crucial for understanding the mechanism by which elementary particles acquire mass. It consists of two main terms: a kinetic term that governs the dynamics of the Higgs field and its interaction with other fields, and a potential term that dictates the ground state of the Higgs field, leading to spontaneous symmetry breaking and mass generation.
higgs-lagrangian.intuitive_summary: The Higgs Lagrangian quantifies how the Higgs field propagates and interacts, ultimately giving mass to other fundamental particles through its non-zero vacuum expectation value.
higgs-lagrangian.interpretation: The Higgs Lagrangian is composed of two principal terms. The first term, –(D_{μ} Φ)† (Dµ Φ), represents the kinetic energy and interaction of the Higgs field. Here, Φ is the Higgs doublet, a complex scalar field. The symbol D_{μ} represents the covariant derivative, which accounts for the interaction of the Higgs field with gauge bosons (like photons, W and Z bosons, and gluons) and ensures gauge invariance. The dagger symbol † denotes the Hermitian conjugate. This term effectively describes how the Higgs field moves and interacts with the electroweak and strong forces. The second term, –V(Φ), is the Higgs potential. This term is responsible for the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the electroweak symmetry. Typically, this potential has a 'Mexican hat' shape, meaning it has a minimum not at Φ = 0, but at a non-zero value. When the Higgs field settles into this minimum, known as the vacuum expectation value (VEV), it breaks the electroweak symmetry, and interactions with this VEV give mass to the W and Z bosons, as well as fermions like electrons and quarks, through Yukawa couplings.
higgs-lagrangian.symmetry_origin: The Higgs Lagrangian originates from the principle of gauge invariance, a fundamental symmetry of nature that underlies the electroweak and strong interactions. The covariant derivative D_{μ} is introduced to maintain this gauge invariance when the Higgs field interacts with gauge fields. The specific form of the Higgs potential V(Φ) is chosen to lead to spontaneous symmetry breaking, a mechanism first proposed by Higgs, Englert, Brout, Guralnik, Hagen, and Kibble, to explain how the W and Z bosons acquire mass while the photon remains massless.
higgs-lagrangian.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the Higgs field amplitude Φ approaches zero, the potential term V(Φ) dictates the behavior. If V(0) is positive (as in the standard 'Mexican hat' potential), the vacuum state is unstable and the field tends to move towards its minimum. If the kinetic term (D_{μ} Φ)^† (D^μ Φ) is negligible (e.g., for a static field), the system seeks to minimize V(Φ). As the energy density approaches infinity, the kinetic term dominates, implying high kinetic energy and rapid fluctuations of the Higgs field.
